Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 7 to amend the Criminal Code-holding of public games for charitable objects.
He said: This bill is introduced at the request of municipalities and church, charitable and patriotic bodies. It makes legal certain public games, such as euchre, cribbage, whist and five hundred in rooms or places to which admission is charged, and provides that such rooms or places shall not be deemed to be common gaming houses as they now are. The privilege is frequently sought to raise funds for relief work by social, church, charitable and patriotic organizations and mayors and wardens have been granting permits to raise funds for these worthy objects. This form of permit was not allowed when the code was drafted thirty years ago, and the object of the amendment is to make it legal now for these charitable objects. The privilege when granted will be under the direct control of the civil and local authorities. The city council of Toronto on December 16, 1924, passed a resolution that the necessary steps be taken to apply to the Dominion parliament for this amendment. The petition was sent to Ottawa in January, 1925, asking that this proposed amendment become law, and the matter, I am told, has also been passed upon by the municipal unions.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

(Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), after repeated solicitations from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy), took the plunge and declared himself in favour of free trade for Canada. I ventured to say that in that regard the hon. member occupied a position of isolation and I am still of the same opinion. I would be very much interested to know if any other Progressives in the House are ready to place themselves on record in the same way as the hon. member for Rosetown did yesterday. I take it for granted that none of them is rushing to do so. I would like to know if the leader of the Progressive

party, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), will declare that he is in favour of free trade for Canada.
I would suggest that the hon. member go on with his speech.

I wish to assure the hon. gentleman that that is precisely what I intend to do. But you will notice how we have manifested the characteristics of the two races represented respectively by the hon,. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), the one speaking as an impulsive Welshman and the other as a canny, cautious Scot. Now the hon. member for Rosetown had a good deal to say about the manufacturers of this country, whom he described by some pretty harsh names; I believe the epithets parasites and bloodsuckers or words of the same significance were used. At all events one would readily conclude from his remarks that the hon. member had not very much love for the manufacturers. According to that hon. gentleman the heads of industries :n this country are bleeding the public and especially the farmers through the exorbitant profits that they are making. The hon. member for Rosetown is a shining light of the Progressive party, a follower of such a man as Hon. Thomas A. Crerar who was at one time leader of that party and who holds the position of president of the United Grain Growers' Company. I desire to call the attention of the House and the attention particularly of my hon. friend from Rosetown and gentlemen from the west to a few figures I have here which indicate the attitude of the company, of which the hon. member's former leader is the president, towards exorbitant profits. According to evidence given in this very building and which I have under my hand, Mr. Rice Jones, who occupied the position of manager of the United Grain Growers' Company, informed the public that the president of that company was drawing a salary of $15,000 per annum, the manager $13,000, the assistant manager $11,000, the western manager $5,200 and the secretary $5,000. That is to say, five officials were drawing a salary of $49,200 per year. The same gentleman informed us further that the profits of that company in 1916-17 amounted to $S44,401, or 44.92 per cent; that the profits in 1915-16 were $855,288, or 62.2 per cent; and that in 1917-18. when they had less grain to handle, the profits amounted to $441,769, or 19.7 per cent. In other words, their profits in three years amounted to $2,141,458, or an average of 42.41 per cent each year.

Mr. Rice Jones told us also in his evidence that the subsidiary company, the New York Export Company, on a capitalization of $100,000 had profits in one year amounting to $530,000 or 530 per cent. In five years the shortages in handling grain amounted to 3,S00 bushels, not a very large amount; but in order to cover these shortages they underweighed the grain of the farmers so that they had overages to the extent of 357,000 bushels. In other words, they secured themselves by taking 100 bushels of grain out of the farmers in order to cover a loss of one bushel. They sold these overages, this extra grain, for $418,000 and put the money into the treasury.
Mr. Rice Jones further stated that this company was engaged not only in handling grain but in handling, as well, farm machinery, binder twine, flour, coal and so on, and that they made handsome profits on each of these articles. It is well for the House to understand that in each of their elevators, of which they have hundreds, there is a man employed to handle the grain, who also acts as agent for the company. If a farmer sends in word that he wants a mower, all the agent has to do is to write a letter to the company and ask them to send on the mower. There 'S an outlay on the part of the company of three cents for postage of the letter, while another three cents may be spent on a letter to the farmer notifying him of the arrival of the machine. The farmer comes to get that piece of machinery and he knows before he leaves home that he has to have the cash in his pocket to pay for it because, as Mr. Rice Jones said, all of this business is done on a strictly cash basis. They were taking no chances whatever with bad accounts. So that all told they were out of pocket only eight or nine cents in postage in doing this business for the farmer.
Now what I want to impress upon the House is this. The president of the United Grain Growers' Company occupied a prominent position in this House and in the political life of Canada for many years, and on many occasions from his place in parliament very strongly denounced protection, condemning for instance the duty of 12J per cent on binders and mowers as taking money out of the pockets of the farmers; and one would naturally think that such a company, handling machinery as they were, running no risks in the matter of bad accounts, and incurring an outlay of only a few cents on each transaction, would have sold the machinery to the farmers without trying to get extra money out of them. But what do we find? In 1921. under the Conservative government, the tariff on binders and mowers was I2i per cent,

I call special attention to the latter statement inasmuch as both Liberals and Progressives are advocating a

Again, I find that the profits of the United Grain Growers' Grain Company on these sixteen implements, according to the sworn evidence of Mr. Rice Jones, was 21.06 per cent. And the profits on the same implements squeezed out of the farmers by the United Grain Growers' Company would amount to $193.63. I call attention to this for the reason that the hon. member for Rosetown, who is not alone in this regard, has expressed himself in very strong language in denunciation of the manufacturers as parasites who extort undue profits from the people and especially from the farmers. What does the hon. gentleman want me to withdraw? I did not say he had deleted it; I said he might say something and might have it deleted. However, I will at once accept the hon. gentleman's statement that he had nothing to do with the leaving out of anything from Hansard. As far as I am concerned, I do not want to quarrel over a little thing like that.
But, Mr. Speaker, what is the position of the hon. member for Rosetown? He comes into this House and from the mountain tops of his own self-esteem he looks down through the fogs and mists which he has himself created and regards with disdain the members of the two old parties, who, whatever their faults, have done all that has been done to make this country progress. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that neither he nor the leader of his party can point to one single thing that their party has done in the direction of national progress. As to the fallacious free trade theories' that the hon. member still clings to with, I might say, tenacity, I will discuss them in a general way with respect not only to the country from which he came but also with respect to our relations with the United States.
I am pleased to note, Mr. Speaker, that several hon. gentlemen, whom I knew very well as humble members like myself when I was here four years ago, have been promoted to the seats of the mighty. I refer first to the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), who is now Minister of Customs. Honours have come to that gentleman before. After the election of 1917, during which he denounced the Borden government and all its works in most vigorous language, he was not averse
to accepting an honourable position under that government and was Deputy Speaker from 1919 to 1921. Rumour also was rife at the time that he would not require to be urged very strongly to accept a cabinet position. However, rumours, like newspaper reports, may be misleading. At all events, the hon. gentleman now is Minister of Customs, and whatever temptations may have assailed him in the past, of this I am quite certain, that he will be true and loyal to the Liberal party-at least, so long as that party remains in power.
Now, the hon. Minister of Customs paid a very warm tribute to ex-Premier King. He referred to his fine, his delicate sense of honour. I recall that Mr. King pledged his word of honour to a certain platform adopted by the Liberal party in 1919, and later he exhibited his fine sense of political honour by referring to that platform on the floor of this House as nothing but a "chart." Then we had his Richmond Hill speech, in which he gave a very distinct pledge to the people, and has since repudiated it. We have also his reference to the Progressives and the sessional indemnity-another exhibition of that delicate sense of honour which, I have no doubt, will be duly appreciated by all the members of that party. Then we have him preparing a speech for His Excellency, and giving out that speech to the press before the Governor General had a chance to read it in the Senate. No other prime minister in the history of Canada has ever possessed such a fine, such a delicate sense of honour as that.
Then we have a still further exhibition of that fine sense of honour. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) moved an amendment to the Address. That amendment, according to all precedent, is a motion of want of confidence in the government. There was consternation in the Liberal camp, because a number of Progressives had declared themselves as having no confidence in this government. Mr. King was sent for, there was a consultation, and he informed his followers that he possessed a certain precious box of ointment that he used as balm for wounded political consciences, an ointment that he had applied with considerable success on many occasions. This box of conscience ointment was sent over to the Progressive camp, where some eighteen members were gathered, and finally it was decided by sixteen or seventeen of that number that they did not stand in need of any conscience balm, since they did not have any consciences to balm. So they generously said,

I am doubtful, Mr. Speaker, whether the Minister of Customs is or can be regarded as competent to judge as to what constitutes political honour. I take that view because of the speech delivered by that hon. gentleman in Montreal, in which he said all that had been discussed at Ottawa was whether a Governor General from England -or if we are to accept his correction, His Excellency, referring to the same person-should decide, or whether the people should choose. He followed that statement by a further remark in which the inference is quite clear. He said that the government would consider itself beaten only by an adverse decision of the people in a general election. "If they, the Progressives, persist in running too fast, we shall not ask for their help any more, and it will be the duty of Premier King to ask for a dissolution of parliament."

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend will allow me to interrupt. The Minister of Customs is not now in his seat, but in fairness to him does not my hon. friend recall that the Minister of Customs, from his place in parliament, said that he had been mis-reported and made a correction in regard to that speech?

I think, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. gentleman did not catch exactly what I said. The Minister of Customs did correct himself, and said that instead of using the words "Governor General from England" he had used the words "His Excellency." I mentioned that when I gave his words. My hon. friend did' not catch what I said. But the Minister of Customs made no correction whatever of the second quotation which I gave. It is true that he has endeavoured to make some explanation with regard to the matter, but to quote the words of the Hon. Edward Blake, it seems to me that he has aggravated his offence by the hypocritical character of his denial. There is no doubt of what is meant by the hon. Minister of Customs. His words contain a double threat, or an intimation amounting to a threat to members of this House that if things are not done as the government wish, there will be a dissolution. It amounts to a threat in another way as well. It is clearly a threat, by plain inference from the words, to His Excellency the Governor General, that unless he does what the remnant of this government says should be done, they are ready to raise the cry of 
autonomy, I suppose, or something along that line. I do not think members of this House are going to submit to threats, and it strikes me that the last man on the face of the earth at the present time who could possibly be intimidated against pursuing the course dictated by honour would be Byng of Vimy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to another hon. member of this House, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), whose undeveloped mind naturally seeks expression in nursery rhymes. He asked the question as to who killed Cock Robin-Cock Robin, of course, being the government. That is not a very difficult question to answer, it was not a case of assassination at all, but mainly one of political suicide. Cock Robin killed himself, although it is quite true that the Conservative party assisted very materially. After the battle of October 29 was over, the Big .Chief and eight of his lesser chiefs were amongst the slain, and the tom-toms were beating outside many a Grit wigwam for the warrior who had been sent to the happy hunting grounds. The Conservative party did play a large part in bringing about that defeat. They did lift some scalps, if I may use the language of the hon. member for Quebec South, but they waged war against the chiefs, and made no war against the papooses of the tribe, so the hon. member for Quebec South was perfectly safe. The hon. member has credited me with the desire to carry the scalp Of the government at my belt back to the lodge. .1 want to assure the hon. gentleman that we decorate the walls of our lodge rooms with emblems which we regard as sacred because of their associations and memories. Notwithstanding that this government has been claiming the divine right to rule with or without the consent of the people, I have not come to the point where I recognize the sacredness of their claim. At all events I want to assure the hon. member for Quebec South that I would' not decorate the walls of an outbuilding with a scalp covering a mind of such narrow dimensions as his.
There were certain outstanding features, Mr. Speaker, of the last election which I desire to call to the attention of the House. The election of 1921 resulted in the return to this House of 51 Conservatives with a definite and clear-cut policy; the election of 117 Liberals, each with a policy of his own and with only one plank in common, namely, their desire for office; and the election of 65 Grits who called themselves Progressives, and whose idea of progress was to stand still or walk backward. The election of 101 Liberals on October 29 last, Mr. Speaker, is the full measure of the

The Address-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
public confidence in the King government. The election of 144 members to this House representing other parties is the measure of the public's want of confidence in that government. In the election of 1921 ithere were 117 Liberals elected, less than a majority of the House, and they only had 41.5 per cent of the popular vote. Those figures indicate to me that farming conditions were not satisfactory in twenty-four of the states, and that farming was going along very nicely in the other twenty-four states.
What did I find further? I found that the twenty-four states which showed a decrease in the number of farms and in improved farm acreage are nearly all northern or middle states, with a climate about the same as we have in Canada. I think I would be near right in saying that those twenty-four states contain between 75 and 80 per cent of the total population of the United States, and therefore they have an advantage in having a market in the urban centres. But the farmers in those states are at this disadvantage; they have to compete with the farmers of the southern states, and of California, and so on, where the climate is mild, where the stock can run out the year round, and where the farmers do not have to invest large sums of money in barns and stables, where also they can produce two or three crops a year to one in the northern states or in Canada. What resulted from this state of affairs? The farmers of these twenty-four states practically all of them north of the 40th parallel, presented a message to congress. They said: "We are forced to compete with the farm products of the states which have a mild climate. Of course, we must submit to that, because we are a part of the same country, but we want to tell you that it places us at a disadvantage, and we do protest against being forced to submit also to competition from Canada, New Zealand, Australia and other countries of the world." And it was on the demand of the organized farmers in these northern states that the Fordney-McCumber tariff was passed for the express purpose of giving them protection against the products of other countries. But they cannot find one, because this is the only country in the world which has lowered its tariff since the war. All other countries have raised theirs. We find our young men leaving Canada because they cannot get work and crossing the lije to the most highly protected country on the face of the globe where they can get work. Does that convey no lesson to hon. gentlemen opposite? If it does not, I must regard them as being absolutely hopeless.
Take the matter of our imports from and our exports to the United States under the tariff as it exists to-day. The farmers of the United States in 1924 sold an average of S12.58 worth of American farm products to every man, woman and child in Canada. That is what our nine million people bought of them. What did the 110,000,000 people from the United States buy from our farmers? ,An average of 96 cents per capita. That is the situation existing under the policy followed by the party opposite, and that is a condi-.tioen which should be rectified at the earliest possible moment. The way to rectify it is for hon. gentlemen opposite to play the game, acknowledge their defeat, acknowledge that the country does not want them on the government benches, and resign and get out.
The other day the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) spoke of inducing our Canadians to return and go on the land, and he added the remark that immigration and repatriation .could not be successful unless supplemented by other policies which would aid in keeping Canadian farmers on the land. With that sentiment I am in entire agreement; but how have the hon. gentleman and his party supplemented .those policies? What steps have they taken to endeavour to make it worth while for our ,Canadian boys to stay on the farm? By opening our doors to Australian and New Zealand1 products; Iby keeping the tariff so 
low that it allows the farm products of other .countries to step over easily and enter Canada in competition with our own. I can come to oo other conclusion than that the policy followed! by this government and evidently supported by members of the Progressive party is one which tells the farmers of Canada in plain words: "You do not amount to anything so far as this country is concerned." We propose a policy of fair-play to the farmers of Canada, a policy which will make them feel that they have behind them a government which will guarantee to them, so far as legislation can, the first place for their products in the home market. That is fair. Anything less than that is not fair. I cannot understand the attitude of those who sometimes talk about free trade as their policy. That is a misnomer, because free trade presupposes a free exchange between two countries. But the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite and of the Progressives, as expressed on the platform and called free trade, is a policy, not of free trade, but of free imports, a policy which says: "We propose to open the doors of Canada to the surplus production of the world so far as the farmers are concerned, while all other countries have their doors closed against our farm products." That is their policy, and against that policy, as the representative of an agricultural constituency, I enter my strongest and most vigorous protest.

The Address-Mr. Marcil
As I mention the mover and seconder of the present Address I am reminded that, in about eight or ten days' time, twenty-five years will have elapsed since I was called upon to second the Address which was moved in 1901 by the hon. member for South Wellington (Air. Guthrie). As I glance over the House on the present occasion I see besides yourself, Air. Speaker, two gentlemen opposite, the father of the House in the person of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) and the hon. member for South Wellington, and on this side, three members, my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and my hon. friend from Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tobin), and the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Delisle), who are all that remain of the parliament that met in 1901. A regiment and more of members of parliament have passed through this House after giving their service to the country; some have gone to a better world and others to different fields of occupation, leaving in Hansard the record of their doings-because without Hansard their eloquence would be lost.
I am glad to be able to say a few words before six o'clock in support of the policy enunciated in the Speech from the Throne, not that it needs very much support on my part, for it speaks for itself. But before I discuss the subject I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Fontenac-Addington (Air. Edwards), who like myself has matured with years in the manner of his delivery and has given us a calm speech that deserves careful consideration. In striking contrast with former speeches of his own, in other days when like myself he was more fiery and rather more combative, he has nevertheless expounded very clearly the policy of the Conservative party, with which I am bound to say at the outset I cannot at all agree. Apart from a few of his personal allusions to some members of the House, the rest of his speech is worthy of him and of the great constituency which he represents and which in the past has been represented in this House by some distinguished men.
As I look into the Speech from the Throne which I had the honour to discuss in seconding the Address which was moved by the hon. member for South Wellington on February 11, 1901, I find by reference to Hansard of that day that the hon. gentleman, then as now one of the most gifted speakers in parliament, outlined very briefly but concisely the position of the Conservative party. Previous to 1896 the Conservative party, as he described it, was a government battling against adversity, whereas after 1806 it was an opposition battling against prosperity. That, I think, compares to some extent with the present 14011-33i
situation. We have a very combative opposition to-day, an opposition more numerous by far than we had in the last parliament; and as it is the meaning and intent of British constitutional government that the only means by which proper and sound government may be obtained is to have a sound, strong, healthy opposition, I do not object to the number of hon. gentlemen who compose the present opposition. Like ourselves, they are representatives of the people. But while they have doubled their numbers in the last election and have returned to parliament with greatly enhanced strength, they do not constitute the majority of the House. The Prime Minister was therefore well advised in asking His Excellency to consult parliament, which is a high court, as to who should carry on the affairs of the country. The mere fact that a party obtains a majority in the country means nothing; it is the number of members elected to parliament who speak for the people at large. Many members sit here representing a minority of the electors, while other members represent overwhelming majorities. But once they are elected to parliament they represent not only their respective constituencies but the whole country, because the tradition of parliament is that a member of parliament, having taken his seat in the House, is no longer the representative of his riding and his riding alone but is the representative at the same time of every constituency in the land1. For that reason I am glad to see in this new parliament so large [DOT] a number of young men on both sides, men who have come here intent on doing their duty and serving their country as best they can. And that is one of the great obligations that rest upon us. Many years ago, when I was a much younger man than I am to-day, the province of Ontario was represented in this parliament by men of outstanding ability. I need not mention their names; for they are familiar to every resident of Ontario. But during a long interim men of the best talents seemed to have given up politics as a vocation and to have gone into other callings. For various reasons a large number of very able -men drifted into the learned professions or into business or other callings and were thus prevented from coming 'into parliament. The country to-day however is glad, I am Sure, to know that we have in this parliament again men of marked ability in all walks of life,-business men, professional men and men from the land. And when I speak of the representatives of agriculture I must say that conditions to-day are different from those that obtained twenty-five
The Address-Mr. Marcil

years ago. At that time we iiad no groups in parliament and the Department of Agriculture was administered not particularly by men who were well versed in the science of agriculture but sometimes by lawyers or doctors. Now, however, we have with us the educated farmer, the farmer who has made a special study of his particular science and who is able to give us the information we need in the interests of agriculture.
Canada is such a large country that it is almost impossible for one to become familiar with all the conditions that call for legislative action in this House. I have had the honour for a quarter of a century of representing a constituency by the Atlantic and 10 my shame I must admit that I have never been west of Winnipeg; 1 have never been across the Rocky Mountains or on the prairies. The reason is that, having spent the winter in Ottawa, I generally find it imperative that I should go to the Atlantic coast in the summer to recuperate if I hope to begin another session when the winter comes again. But although I have never been west I have met from the west, *as indeed from Ontario and other parts of the country, men who have done a real service to Canada, and I hope in this parliament, be sts duration long or short, that we shall have a courteous debate at all times. After all, our first duty is to our country, and although we may enjoy vigorous debate, so long as it is carried1 on in parliamentary language I think Canada will not suffer.
To show the progress that the Dominion has made, I may be permitted to refer to the Speedh from the Throne in 1901, which among other things mentioned the return of our contingent from South Africa, the coming visit of the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall, the display made by Canada in the cold storage section of the Paris exhibition, the development of the St. Lawrence, and the favourable increase in our trade. Twenty-five years have elapsed, and some of those subjects are still under discussion. At that time we discussed free trade and protection, moderate .tariff and high tariff, the condition of agriculture and so on, and I suppose we shall continue to discuss those subjects for many years to come. In 1901 the member for South Wellington, in his speech on the Address-which of course was a eulogy of the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier-said that the McKinley tariff, which had then been brought into effect, was in some respects a blessing to Canada, an that it had put our people on their mettle and had brought us to realize that a high tariff in the United States was

not altogether an unfortunate thing for Canada. We had always deplored the high tariff of our neighbours, yet during the fifteen years of the Laurier regime-which to-day stands as the golden era of our prosperity- the McKinley tariff did not prevent this country from being prosperous. The member for South Wellington gave as a reason that our natural resources placed Canada at all times in a more favourable position than any other country in the world. I think he was right.
On that occasion Mr. Robert Borden-now Sir Robert Borden-made his debut as leader of the Conservative party in the House. Having been chosen only the night before as leader, he could not be expected to expound the .policy of his party, but he gave as a reason for our prosperity the fact that favourable .conditions were world-wide. Of course, that was true then, and is true now. When the world is prosperous Canada must necessarily be favourably affected; when the world is not prosperous naturally Canada will be more or less adversely affected. Canada has emerged from the war in a much better condition than any other belligerent country, and I believe every conscientious member will admit the correctness of my statement.
When in August, 1914, we were called here, at a few days' notice, to declare whether Canada should enter the war, I had no mandate from my constituency; the question had not been discussed at the general election in 1911. On that occasion we had discussed reciprocity and the naval question. As I say, we had no mandate to declare war in 1914, but it must be said to the credit of the parliament of that day that every member agreed that the moment war was declared upon Great Britain it was the duty of Canada to join the Mother Country, and we went voluntarily to her assistance without a single dissenting voice. That will always stand to the credit of Canada. To-day we are mourning the loss of Cardinal Merrier. During the war no man played a greater part or gave a more inspiring example of devotion to God and country than did the heroic cardinal of Belgium. I had .the honour shortly after the war of meeting him at the city hall in Montreal, when the city greeted him on his way to the United States. I informed him that Canada had raised, equipped and sent overseas 600,000 men, and had incurred a war debt of nearly a billion dollars. His Eminence was dumbfounded at the extent of our participation in the war, and almost with tears in his eyes he thanked those who were present

The Address-Mr. Marcil
for Canada's assistance to Belgium in her glorious struggle against her invaders.
The war period was a trying one to Canada, but it brought a transient prosperity- trade boomed and everybody sold his products at a very high price. In my own constituency farm produce sold at whatever prices the owner cared to fix. But during the war several eminent authorities, more especially Sir George Foster, warned us repeatedly that there would be a period of deflation after the war and that we should be prepared for that financial stringency and commercial depression. It came after the signing of the Armistice and was at its worst, perhaps, in 1921. We have not got over its effect yet, but we are gradually emerging into a better position, and gooner than anyone expected. I have read somewhere that after Waterloo it took twenty years for Europe to right itself economically. If we get through in half that time I think we will be doing well. I see that the total trade of Canada in 1920 was $2,639,726,135; in 1921 it dropped to $1,616,172,764; in 1922 there was a slight increase, $1,660,587,106; in 1923 there was a still further increase, $1,911,559,638; in 1924 it dropped slightly, $1,878,756,189, and in 1925 it made a splendid recovery, $2,171,366,141. This shows that Canada at the present time is fairly prosperous. Our balance of trade is $400,000,000 to the good, and it is increasing steadily. Of course, there will be complaints from some quarters-from the manufacturers and from the farmers. Sir Wilfrid Laurier used to say that if we had no troubles in this world we would not need governments, for governments existed to right troubles. When complaints do not come from Cape Breton, they come from British Columbia. In the old days many and many a night have I spent in this chamber listening to debates on the oriental question; that no longer troubles us at it did in those days. Latterly we have been giving more attention to western affairs. The great leader of the Conservative party at the time the Canadian Pacific railway was completed said the west was destined to become the granary of the world. And after all, the west is the great hope of this country. Canada will never occupy the position she should in relation to her neighbour .to the south unless we fill up our vast western spaces. But- a small portion of the west is settled at the present time, and if we are to solve our difficulties and, as mentioned in the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), provide employment for our industrial population, we must
develop the enormous agricultural resources of the west, because agriculture is the basis pf everything.
What was the outstanding feature of the success of the Laurier policy for fifteen years? It was the immigration policy put into effect by Clifford Sifton, a western man, by which he brought to the west over a million people, making a million nevi customers for Canada, a million people to duplicate, triplicate and quadruplicate the orders sent to manufacturers in Toronto, Hamilton, Montreal, and other manufacturing centres. These manufacturers worked night and day at that time, and I hope the time is not far distant when that condition will again prevail. All those who know the present state of affairs know that Canada is now on a fair way to prosperity. The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington read an extract from a speech by Sir Herbert Holt, president of the Royal Bank. If you listened to those words, you will remember that Sir Herbert Holt concluded by saying that to come to the relief of industry in Canada there must be a scientific study of the tariff. That is what the present administration proposes to do, among other things. The Speech from the Throne deals with various other matters which have been before us for a long time. One of these I will mention, the consolidation of departments. The Canadian taxpayer is immensely interested in the income tax and other taxes which he has to pay. Our taxation here has not been reduced as has that of the United States and England. We are still paying a very high rate. The cost of government-it is the fault of confederation, if you like-to the people of Canada is very high. Apart from our federal government we have nine provincial governments and a thousand municipal governments. We 'have in our administration a number of departments which should have disappeared a long time ago; many of them should be merged because they do similar work. I am glad to know that the government is going to take up the matter of merging some of these departments in order that the cost of government may be reduced.
A simplified form of accounting is also proposed. It has always been a great drawback to the Canadian student of our system of government to be confronted with these huge blue books, appearing twelve months after the fiscal year has ended, the French translations of which sometimes do not appear for another twelve months. Very often the ordinary Canadian is not familiar with t'he cost of government and with the economic conditions under which he lives, and if the
The Address-Mr. Marcil

government can bring about a simplified system of making this information ipublie they will have rendered valuable service, because the salvation of a country depends upon the public interest taken in its government. Nations have the government they deserve, a wise man has said. We know that in every general election, sometimes half the voters do not even go to the polls. Since the female suffrage has been added things have been made worse, probably because in our province at least we had not been accustomed to it. The legislature of Quebec rejected it, believing that the French-Canadian mother, with a reputation for raising ten or twelve children, was busily enough engaged in home duties without going into the streets to discuss politics. But although Quebec rejected that measure, it has been imposed upon us by a majority vote of parliament; it is now tihe law of the land and must be respected. In a mixed constituency a large number of the English women go to the polls and vote-they were accustomed to doing so during the war; but in our French municipalities the women do not go to the polls in such large numbers. Be sides, the granting of the vote to women has not been looked upon with favour in Quebec. However it exists, and if the government can foster public interest and provide every voter in Canada, male or female, with the opportunity of becoming better acquainted with our system of government and with the cost of government, it will be doing a great work. We would then have a barometer by which we could gauge public opinion. If we can have the figures plainly set forth showing the cost of government in a manner easily understood, we will go far towards arousing public opinion. You know that when a man's pocket is affected he becomes more interested.

Mr. Speaker, there is a
paragraph in the Speech from the Throne to which I wish to allude in particular, as it is of great importance to the province of Quebec. It is the one relating to repatriation and reads as follows:	(
Measures will be taken to further the retention on the land of our existing agricultural population, to encourage the return to rural parts of urban dwellers *possessed of agricultural experience, and the repatriation of Canadians now living in other countries. Special arrangements will be proposed for settlement on Crown Lands.
[Mr. Marcil.3
As far back as I can remember the flow of immigration to and from the United States has been chronic. When we consider that there are between two and three million Canadians in the United States, it is evident that this movement has been going on for many years. I remember many years ago attending a banquet of the Canadian Club in Boston, at which Curtis Guild, the Governor of Massachusetts, told us he was of the opinion that there were in Boston enough Canadians and descendants of Canadians, especially from the Maritime provinces, to elect the mayor. That state of affairs has always existed and always will exist in some degree; for individuals will go from one country to the other according to the advantages the respective countries offer. There was a time without a doubt in the United States after the war when that country offered great opportunities, and many Canadians took advantage of that state o*f affairs and crossed the line. Though many .of them have since returned, I hope that a sincere effort will be made by the government to bring back as many Canadians as possible, and more especially to bring back to the land; for that is the salvation of the country. In order to do that, the country must be made more attractive. The provinces are doing their fair share in this respect, and the Dominion parliament some years ago voted considerable sums of money to that end.
To make the country attractive you must have, first, good roads. You must have good communications, easy access to the city and to the markets. Then you must have such other facilities as the provinces can afford; and in that regard the Dominion dhould try to assist as far as possible. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) can do a very important work in this respect. In our province he is -working hand in hand with the provincial government to further agriculture in Quebec.
I was glad to learn from the figures quoted this afternoon by the hon. member for Fron-tenac-Addington that Quebec leads the Dominion in the quantity of butter and cheese manufactured. The butter factory has become a regular institution in each of our parishes. The farmers get together, take in their milk, and go in for butter making. Quite a number of them have gone in for cheese making as well, but butter seems to be the chief production of the rural parts. It sells readily, brings ready cash, and refrigeration facilities are always available. Transportation facilities are provided by the Intercolonial and other railways, and a consider-

The Address-Mr. Marcil
able sum of money has come to the fanners in this way. But other means must be taken to try and keep our farmers on the land.
I see that one paragraph in the Speech from the Throne announces that:
With a view to affording such remedies as may appear to be practical and appropriate, the government also propose to appoint a royal commission to inquire fully into the claims that the rights of the Maritime provinces in regard to the operation of the Intercolonial Railway have not been observed, and that in regard to transportation, immigration, and other economic factors these provinces have suffered prejudicially, in their position under confederation.
This investigation should not be limited to the Maritime provinces, but should extend to the eastern part of Quebec, the maritime part of Quebec and the Gaspe Peninsula, which you, Mr. Speaker, and I have had the honour to represent in this House for many years. We have a large and growing population, and the problem is to keep the boys at home. Give them remunerative work at home, work on the land; provide them with easy access to markets, and that will be the solution of many of our difficulties. If we can keep them on the land and secure markets for them, we shall have made immense progress. Important as immigration from outside may be,
I have no doubt that a Canadian would be preferred to one of any other nationality, because he is to the manner born; he is a native of the country and has the traditions of his native land at heart. We have had very few immigrants from Europe, France and Belgium, since the war, though these countries had previously been sending a good many people to our shores. We are getting some from the British Isles. The government has entered into an arrangement with the British government and the Canadian railways in reference to bringing immigrants to Canada, and the result should be a desirable increase of our population. Hon. members must never forget that if we can increase the trade of the country and secure immigration, Canada will be on the high road to prosperity. Anything that will tend in that direction will be furthered by the government. In the appointment of the commission which has been suggested they have taken a forward step and the matter will be fully considered.
The right hon. leader of the opposition made a statement of interest to the farmer when he said that if he came into office he would endeavour to equalize the American and Canadian tariffs on agricultural production. There is no doubt that on some articles the American tariff appears to be much higher than ours, but it is difficult for a layman to express an opinion offhand as to exactly what should be done; only those who are experts
can deal properly with the situation. The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington seems to be of the opinion that the farmer should be given a preference wherever it is possible to give it to him-not only the farmer, but the Canadian manufacturer and the Canadian people in general. Well, we have had that policy for years. Tariffs are not unchangeable; they are subject to alteration from time to time. We may have a high tariff against a certain article for a time, but it may be changed in a year or two. If a foreign country can give you something that you consider worth having, you may have to alter your tariff. Tariffs may be changed according to the situation and policies of other countries. I believe in the stability of tariffs, because when men invest their money in an enterprise they want to feel assured that they will receive a fair return for their investment.
There are other matters dealt with in the Speech from the Throne to which I do not wish to refer at any length, but I think there are one or two paragraphs which should not be passed over.	[DOT]
I will refer now to the clause relating to the completion of the Hudson Bay railway.
I have had the advantage of hearing this matter discussed ever since it was brought up in parliament many years ago. The idea at that time was to set aside a part of the prairies, sell the lands, and with the pt.meeds of the sale to construct the railway. I am not in a position to say whether the proceeds would be enough to cover the expenditure, but the amount of money which has been expended on that enterprise has been so great that I think we are bound to complete it. I am convinced, therefore, that the government is taking the right course in the matter, and probably my hon. friends opposite would do the same if they were in power. The farmer in western Canada is a long distance from the seaboard; he is entitled to all the help and assistance we can give him, and he should be afforded an outlet for his products. In the old days we had only Montreal as an outlet. Now we have Vancouver, and later on we will have the Hudson Bay railway, for whatever it is worth.
The problem of preventing the diversion of grain through American channels has been a subject of discussion for many years, and it still remains unsolved. The construction of the Transcontinental railway in northern Ontario and Quebec was taken up in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's time, the idea being to develop the northern part of the country; to give the country a greater width, so to speak; to develop the immense resources of
The Address-Mr. Marcil

northern Ontario and Quebec, and finally to give an outlet to the west. It seems unfortunate that a railway constructed at such tremendous cost and connecting the west with such a fine port as the city of Quebec is not utilized more than it is. The government would be well advised if they took this matter up in earnest with a view to enabling Quebec and the other provinces to take advantage of the facilities afforded by this great railway. I have a great deal of sympathy for the western farmer. He labours hard; he places his crop in the ground and he has to contend with many obstacles. If he sells locally a portion of his crop and exports the remainder of it, he comes in competition with the market of other countries, and the prices are fixed there and not here. He is entitled, I say, to all the country can give him; and in this scheme of immigration and repatriation, if the government is able to offer inducements to bring people into this country, the result will be more conducive to the success of the farmer than anyone else. It is all right to advertise to bring people out to western Canada, but you must be sure they will be able to make a living. In the old days, when Sir Clifford Sifton was a member of the government, we were giving away free homesteads near the railway and offering other attractions, but many of those advantages cannot be had to-day. I think Canada should be prepared to make a sacrifice, even in respect to the Canadian National Railways, in order to further the opening of the west.
The present government are entitled to credit for the way they have handled the Canadian National Railways. At the opening of the last parliament public opinion w^ much divided on that question. Many people from Quebec were opposed to the public ownership of the railway; others from Ontario and Quebec were in favour of it, but we effected a compromise-that was the only basis on which the matter could be arranged. Being a confederation, we called upon everybody to compromise. We all said, "Let us give the Canadian National Railways a fair trial. Let us select an efficient man who can take hold of it and make it a success." Sir Henry Thornton has made good under the trying circumstances in which he has been placed. I cannot resist the temptation of paying my tribute in this connection to the father of the House, the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), who in the olden days was the lone voice in the desert in his advocacy of public ownership, day in and

day out. He advocated public ownership of the hydro-electric proposition in Ontario; and I think we should congratulate the Ontario government on the success of their operations in that respect.
The country is now passing through a trying ordeal, but it will come through successfully. People are looking to the west. The right hon. leader of the government went west to secure a seat. He went there as a connecting link, as a messenger of peace between the east and the west. One thing that would be fatal to this country would be a division between the east and the west. The prosperity of western Canada will inure tc the prosperity of Ontario and all the other eastern provinces, so that we must bring about a closer understanding. I am glad, therefore, that the Prime Minister has decided to ask the electors of Prince Albert to return him to this House, so that he may be in a position to give the west in his own person a perfect guarantee that he is prepared to take up and solve their problems; because without doubt it is in the western part of Canada that the greatest of our problems lies at the present time.
I do not wish to delay the House at any greater length, and I will close by referring to the first two paragraphs in the Speech from the Throne. In one, allusion is made to the election of a Canadian to be president of the sixth assembly of the League of Nations. At a moment when the United States has practically decided to enter the League of Nations, the fact that a Canadian-a citizen of the province of Quebec, I am glad to say; a man who has given long and faithful sendee in the Senate of Canada-should be found worthy of occupying that high position is an incentive to all Canadians to put forth efforts to show the world that Canadians are qualified to fill any position that presents itself.
In the Speech from the Throne of twenty-five years ago, the Address in reply to which was moved by the hon. member for South Wellington and seconded by myself, the first paragraph was an allusion to the death of Queen Victoria, probably the greatest woman who ever occupied the throne of Great Britain. It was during her reign that responsible government was established in Canada. In the first paragraph of the present Speech from the Throne we are called upon to-day to mourn the death of another distinguished woman, the widow of Edward VII, the peacemaker, the man who created the entente eordi-ale between France and England. Foreseeing what might happen some day, he brought

The Address-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskiwin)
about a better understanding between those two great nations. The understanding had its effect in Canada; and a better feeling has prevailed in this country since English and French soldiers fought and bled side by side on the battlefields of France and Flanders in defence of civilization and humanity. In this the beginning of a new parliament we should do all we can to bring about a better understanding among our Canadian people, to cause them to become better acquainted with each other, to destroy provincial barriers so far as possible, and thus to bring about the advancement and prosperity of this great Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, relying upon the patience and indulgence traditionally accorded to new members in this House of Commons, I wish for a few moments to deal with the motion before the Chair. At the outset I desire to concur in the many expressions of confidence and pleasure in your appointment to the high position that you now hold. It is indeed a pleasure to me to congratulate you, Sir, at this time.
I also wish, as is customary, to pay my tribute to the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. It is a great pleasure, Sir, to a western man, or indeed to any Canadian, to read the Speech from the Throne. It points to true progress. It is in every sense of the word a Liberal platform. It has not been challenged by anyone, not even by the right hon. leader of the opposition in his amendment. I believe that the legislative programme it forecasts will help the people generally of this country. True some hon. members are of opinion that there should be a duty on agricultural products. To support their argument they instance our imports from the United States of butter, cheese and flour; but these imports were so insignificant compared to our immense exports of the same products to our neighbours across the line that I am at a loss to understand their desire to forego this profitable business.
I submit, Sir, that if Canada is to progress and become the great country that we believe is her destiny we must put aside sectionalism and present a united front. The west and the east must cease their petty quarreling and compose their differences, and in a spirit of harmony work together for a united Canada. I recognize-we all recognize-that the western prairies are a dominant force in the pro-14011-341

I believe that all immigration to Canada should be under the direct supervision of the Dominion government, co-operating with the provincial governments vvherever they wish to take part.
